newsitem.title: TURKEY: Saudis raid falling world grain market for barley.
newsitem.headline: Saudis raid falling world grain market for barley.

text.p: Saudi Arabia hit the world grain market for over a million tonnes of barley worth $200 million on Monday to take advantage of falling prices and replenish low stocks, grain traders said.
It was one of the single biggest grain purchases by an importing nation so far this year and stopped a recent slide in world prices for the grain in its tracks.
But despite the deal barley prices, which have fallen after soaring to records early this year, will continue to face pressure from a rebound in world crops, analysts said.

"This is a halt to the decrease in prices. But the Saudi purchase will not hold the price for long," Geneva-based consultant James Dunsterville said on the sidelines of a grains conference in southern Turkey.
Europe and Canada have biggger crops this year while ample Australian supplies will start arriving from December.

Traders said Saudi Arabia -- the world's largest barley importer as well as the biggest oil exporter -- had bought 1.4 million tonnes of barley at prices between $146 and $158 per tonne for delivery between October and December.
Farmers mainly in western Europe, but also in Canada, the United States and Australia, are set to benefit from the deal, pieced together by around seven multinational trade firms.

Excluding the cost of transport, the deal works out at some $130 per tonne or more, traders said. Before this year's harvests, when grain stocks were down to their lowest in 20 years, barley prices towered at a record $200 a tonne.
Saudi Arabia uses its oil revenues to import barley for tribesmen to control the kingdom's sprawling animal herds.
The barley is dyed at the port of arrival to distinguish it from the kingdom's own, heavily subsidised, production.
Analysts peg Riyadh's annual barley import needs at around 3.5 million tonnes.
A U.S agricultural official told the conference that Saudi Arabia may increase its strategic imports of the grain.

Mark Sloan, agriculture counsellor at the U.S. embassy in Turkey, said recent cuts in subsidies to Saudi farmers would increase the kingdom's reliance on world markets, despite Middle East grain demand having stabilised this decade.
Saudi Arabia has been forced to review its generous farm subsidy programmes to help close a spending gap caused by thhe cost of financing the 1991 Gulf war aggainst Iraq.

The International Grains Council, a London-based monitor of grain markets, says however that more barley will be available for importers this year, with world produuction rising nearly 10 percent to 163.3 million tonnes.
